book: 054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor
essays: Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory
Area Philosopher (Me!) Is Sick Of The Stupid Debate About Stupid
Jesus Delays Second Coming Because Of Offensive Article
Area Man And Woman Wonder What They Are Good For
A Newspaper Gone to the Dogs . . . Enlightened Dogs
Scientists Find Anomalies In And Then Go Back and Kill Your Grandparents
Gene For Pedantry Same As Gene For Philosophy
World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent
The Onion, Sarcasm, and the Good of Mankind
samples: Sharon M. Kaye's introduction recounts the legend that The Onion got its name from an uncle's suggestion while the founders ate onion sandwiches, then argues the dictionary definition of 'onion' fits perfectly: 'bulbous' things are inherently funny and 'pungent' things penetrate and burn. The Onion's satire is therefore philosophical, she concludes, because philosophers have always been critics of the society in which they live—an uncomfortable wake-up call, like heartburn—and the chapters ahead will 'unpeel' the connections.

Kaye argues that the highest form of ridicule, which The Onion has mastered, targets not stupidity but cheating—specifically 'asscheating,' believing what you want to be true. She reads 'I Believe In Evolution, Except For The Whole Triassic Period' as skewering people who understand Darwin perfectly but exempt humans from evolution because admitting we are just another animal means admitting we die like everything else, the move behind Aquinas-style teleological add-ons that only invite a regress of gods supplying 'extras.' Articles on breast implants, the 'New Nietzschean Diet,' and Tour de France doping all show asscheats artificially inflating their evolutionary fitness; since natural selection stamps every organism with the purpose of survival and reproduction, asscheating is a vice, and ridiculing the asscheats who pollute the gene pool is itself a survival strategy.

Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.

Cuddy stages the generational-decline debate between Mark Bauerlein's The Dumbest Generation and Stephen Johnson's Everything Bad Is Good for You, showing that Onion stories can be marshaled for both sides: Aristophanes complaining that today's audiences 'just don't get me' vindicates the perennial declinist, while 'US Students Lead World in Detention' wryly supports Johnson's sleeper curve. Comparing Bauerlein to Aristophanes and the 'Our Dumb World' entry on Aristotle and Plato's schools closing, he concludes every era teems with idiots, so The Onion could have existed in any century. Because induction from earlier generations' failed predictions cannot settle whether Millennials really are dumber, he suspends judgment and toasts The Onion as the smartest perspective around.

Arp asks why well-placed 'fucks' in Onion headlines like 'Guy In Philosophy Class Needs To Shut The Fuck Up' are funny, and answers with the golden mean traced to Aristotle and Confucius, who both prized self-control and being a good role model to children: swearing is virtuous when it hits the mean between the vice of too much (gangsta rap's every-other-word profanity, the cemetery gardener's rant, Glengarry Glen Ross) and the vice of too little. He sorts Onion stories into vice tables—'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer' illustrates the vice of cowardice, with courage as the hitting-the-mark mean—and concludes that a well-placed fuck is both funny and virtuous precisely because so many people treat the word as taboo.

Hallquist observes that Dan Savage's 'Savage Love' column, syndicated in The Onion, treats 'asshole' not as a mere expletive but as a property that can be discovered, disagreed about, and used to explain behavior—raising exactly the puzzles philosophers raise about morality. He defends an expressivist account modeled on Ayer's: 'Dan Savage is an asshole' expresses an attitude while picking out a range of behavior defined by shared attitudes, and he answers the classic objections (logic requires truth-aptness, moral disagreement seems factual, we ask third parties who the asshole is) by adapting Singer's point that logic applies to commands and attitudes too, and by showing disagreement over assholery is a conflict of attitudes we still have urgent practical reason to resolve. Since the standard arguments against moral expressivism would equally refute this intuitively plausible asshole-expressivism, the objections must fail, giving moral expressivism a modest positive argument.

book: 055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside
essays: We’ve Been Abducted by the Doctor, and We Love It!
Doctor Who and the Ultimate Answer
I Think, Therefore I Exist . . . I Think
We Wouldn’t Be Here Without Time Travel
The Daleks Can Stop the Pyramids from Being Built!
This Is the Age of Steel
They May Not Be Human, but Could Daleks Be People Too
Aww, . . . Poor Monster. Should We Feel Sorry for the Carrionites
A Better Way of Living Your Life
Why the Doctor Is So Special
Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign
Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity
samples: The editors' introduction recounts the show's history from its 1963 premiere (the day after the Kennedy assassination) and the Daleks' first appearance through all eleven Doctors, and describes how companions from Ian and Barbara to Rose, Donna, and Amy were 'abducted' by the Doctor's sense of wonder. It argues that the curiosity and love of adventure the TARDIS inspires in viewer-companions is the very same impulse that drives the love of wisdom, and previews the book's six 'episodes' on personal identity, time travel, logic and science, the Doctor's ethics, existentialism and aesthetics, and the show's cultural meaning.

Stokes uses regeneration and the multi-Doctor episodes ('The Three Doctors', 'The Five Doctors', 'The Trial of a Time Lord') to test theories of personal identity: Locke's memory criterion, Reid's transitivity objection, Parfit's teleporter and 'branch-line' cases, Nozick's closest-continuer theory, four-dimensional person-stages, animalism, and narrative identity. He argues that no objective-continuity account explains why the Fifth Doctor still cares whether he himself survives in 'The Caves of Androzani', and hints that being the Doctor may be a subjective stance in which each incarnation takes ownership of the others as itself.

Littmann mines Who scenarios as hypotheticals that test identity theories: regeneration, natural doubles like Salamander, impersonating Zygons and Chameleons, bodiless beings like Omega and the Great Intelligence, TARDIS jumps that break spatiotemporal continuity, Cassandra possessing the Doctor and Rose, memory theft by Eldrad and the Daleks, and the Master's year as the unrecognizably good Professor Yana. He argues that sameness of body (including the four-dimensional 'worm' of spatiotemporal continuity), the memory criterion, and psychological similarity each fail, leaving the question of what makes the Doctor the Doctor — and you you — open.

Hanley first fixes what is true in the Who canon (treating fiction as pretense), then asks how the Doctor persists when regeneration replaces 'every single cell' and when John Smith's amnesia severs memory in 'Human Nature'. Rejecting bodily continuity (the severed hand of 'The Christmas Invasion'), soul 'pellets', and simple memory (Reid's transitivity problem), he defends neo-Lockean mental continuity plus Nozick's closest-continuer schema to explain why Jackson Lake, the regrown Doctor, and DoctorDonna in 'Journey's End' are not the Doctor, and closes with Parfit's claim that psychological continuity rather than identity is what matters in survival, alongside Lewis's space-time-worm alternative.

Johnson argues that the Platonic-Cartesian soul is refuted by neuroscience (Phineas Gage, Penfield's stimulation studies), and that Locke's memory criterion fails on Reid-style transitivity cases like DoctorDonna and on Bernard-Williams-inspired worry about the amnesiac John Smith, who would still dread the Family of Blood's torture. Parfit's causal-continuity criterion then wrongly makes the meta-crisis Doctor of 'Journey's End' identical with the Tenth, so Johnson defends a four-dimensionalist 'time worm' view on which the Doctors are stages of one person — before a final sorites-style argument (heaps, spin-offs like Torchwood) suggests that 'persons' may not exist at all.

Worley distinguishes logical from empirical possibility (Leonardo's round-square in 'City of Death') and shows that time-travel paradoxes — Leela's self-caused antibodies, the unauthored 'Blink' Easter egg, the Master's Toclafane — can be handled with Zeno-style analysis of contradiction and David Lewis's distinction between external and personal time, under which travelers instantiate rather than rewrite history ('The Visitation', 'The Time Meddler'). He then reads 'Turn Left' and the Doctor's 'alternative time' in 'Pyramids of Mars' through Leibniz's possible worlds and Lewis's actualism about parallel universes, concluding that in 'City of Death' time travel is essential to life on Earth existing at all.

book: 056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat
essays: From the Deserts of Arrakis to the Deserts of Earth
Spice as the Vehicle of Power
The Emergence of Good from Evil
In The Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man . .
samples: A fictional editor's preface presenting the volume as speeches recovered from the Bene Gesserit Archives and the ruins of Dar-es-Balat, gathered for the ten-thousandth anniversary of Leto II's transformation into the God Emperor. It sets up the book's framing conceit: the essays are in-universe commemorations of Paul, Duncan Idaho, and the Dune-times, written by authors who look back in fascination at 'those legendary philosophies' of ancient Earth.

Reads the Gom Jabbar test as Herbert's definition of humanity: Paul endures Mohiam's pain box because a human stays in the trap to turn it on the trapper and protect the species, while an animal only chews off its own leg. The Butlerian Jihad's ban on 'a machine in the likeness of a man's mind' is applied to our own iPod-and-PDA dependence, with Mentat Thufir Hawat showing that losing the machine-crutch 'forced human minds to develop,' in line with Aristotle's phronesis and the politics of the common good (and Plato's contemplation as the core of happiness). The chapter closes by turning the human/animal test on the modern West—Baron Harkonnen-like consumers whose water-hungry beef habit makes us the trap of our own environmental collapse.

Compares Herbert's three eugenics programs: the Bene Gesserit's centuries-long Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (explicitly modeled on the communal breeding of the guardians in Plato's Republic, undone when Jessica bears Paul a generation early and he escapes their control), Leto II's Golden Path breeding for Siona's invisibility to prescience, and the Tleilaxu axolotl-tank immortality that collapses when their Face Dancers out-mimic them. Each program is weighed ethically—Leto as the 'ultimate consequentialist' whose species-saving tyranny invokes Mill's utilitarianism and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means, the Sisterhood as shifting toward Kantian duties against using persons as mere means. Herbert's lesson: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics,' whether aimed at a single person, a single result, or a single agenda.

Built entirely on Clausewitz's 'remarkable trinity'—the balance of people, military, and government—as the framework for war in Dune: Duke Leto's plan to win Fremen support on Arrakis, Muad'Dib's defusal of the Stilgar leadership challenge as a model of trinity-balancing in irregular warfare, and the messianic goal-inflation that unbalances the trinity and unleashes the jihad that kills sixty-one billion. The author, a US Army officer writing as a Mentat of Leto II, applies the same lesson to Afghanistan and post-Saddam Iraq: without a clear, achievable political goal, military force produces unintended consequences no Kwisatz Haderach could fully control.

Stages the paradox of foreknowledge through Paul's prescient dream of meeting Chani and his futile struggle against the foreseen jihad: since knowledge (on Plato's justified-true-belief account) is factive, a known future seems unalterable. It tests the classic escapes—Boethius's God in ever-present eternity and Aquinas's seeing all time 'under the aspect of eternity,' Laplace's demon, Richard Taylor's fatalism—and finds the Atreides oracles are no gods, only probabilistic predictors whose visions fix the possibilities they see. The way out is Anscombe's Intention: like God knowing creation because He authored it, Paul and Leto know their futures practically, as agents whose intentions help decide which possibilities become actual, so freedom survives as terrific responsibility.

Argues the Fremen are 'shockingly American': their Spannungsbogen self-discipline, spiritual self-sufficiency, and endurance of hardship exemplify Emerson's self-reliance, while the jihad's aim of razing the rule of the Great Houses into relations of equals echoes Dewey's democracy as a way of life—faith in the potentialities of every human nature. The parallel runs through the 'American Taliban' John Walker Lindh and Paul's blind walk into the desert, both acting on values Americans prize. Herbert's remark that people surrender judgment to leaders 'wrapped in the myth fabric of society' grounds the pragmatist point that Fremen myth-making, like America's exceptionalist self-image, works—and Alia's 'my brother is pragmatic' seals it.

book: 057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United
essays: Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do
Houston, We Have a Problem, or, What Goes Up Must Come Down
He’s Got to Make His Own Mistakes
Let Your Heart Be the Anchor and the Beat of Your Own Song
Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love
“I Want to Look Around Me Now”
Listen to My Music, and Hear What It Can Do
Does Rush Offer a Way Out
Counterparts Lee’s Voice and Peart’s Drums
Straining the Limits of Machine and Man
There’s Something Here that’s as Strong as Life
samples: The editors' introduction frames Rush as a 'thinking man's band': a cult favorite deliberately outside the mainstream whose fusion of virtuosic, structurally complex music with lyrics on social, scientific, and historical themes triggers both fierce devotion and passionate hatred in listeners. It sketches the band's history from its 1968 Toronto cover-band beginnings through Neil Peart's 1974 arrival and the album-oriented-rock success of Moving Pictures ('Tom Sawyer', 'Limelight'), arguing that Rush's lasting achievements come when thoughtful lyrics and progressive/hard music work together. It invites readers to treat each essay as one voice in an ongoing dialogue and to accept that being different, like Rush, is not a bad thing.

Auxier interleaves a memoir of sneaking off to Rush's 1977 Memphis concert (the Halloween-weekend ruse with his friend Brice, beers at J-Wags Lounge, the first hangover, and the setlist from 'Bastille Day' through '2112') with a philosophical defense of the band. He rejects the charge that Rush is a vehicle for Ayn Rand's objectivism, arguing Rand was a novelist with 'philosophical moments' whose analogy-built system is not philosophy, and that Peart quickly outgrew her influence by Moving Pictures. Working from Susanne Langer, he claims Rush assimilates lyrics to music (so 'Tom Sawyer' and 'Limelight' need no poetic standard), that music is a 'virtualization' of time creating the illusion of felt life, and that Rush's live processed sounds are second-order virtualizations whose only real test is whether the music is good.

Bowman surveys the fifty-four recorded Rush tributes of 1996-2005, from the Barenaked Ladies quoting the 'Tom Sawyer' swagger riff in 'Grade 9' to DJ Z-Trip's trip-hop remix, Disarray's death-metal version, Deadsy's industrial take, and string-quartet translations, arguing that Rush's ambiguous genre coding is what lets this 'musicians' music' travel across mutually exclusive fan communities. He builds his own 'scholarly meta-remix' interleaving six versions of 'Tom Sawyer' in different keys and meters, and reads the 7/4 instrumental section's fate in each cover. Borrowing Robert Walser's claim that musical meanings are grounded in an ideological field where institutions enforce preferred meanings, he concludes that tribute artists find 'refractive, distorted, and disruptive' meanings in Rush, and that progressive rock served as 'substitute classical music' for working- and lower-middle-class fans.

Sheinbaum argues against the assumption that Rush's rhythmic complexity is 'thinking' music opposed to bodily groove, showing through close listening that 'Subdivisions' (7/8 in 2+2+3 groups), 'Limelight' (4/4 and 3/4 bars interleaved), 'Jacob's Ladder' (alternating 5/4 and 6/4), and the 7/8 passages of 'La Villa Strangiato' all groove while the band retains standard eight-bar phrase structures. He treats meter and hypermeter as Western cultural constructions, and reads Rush's metric deviations as a musical image of the individual resisting a 'conformist social order' (citing Chris McDonald on the individualism Rush shares with Ayn Rand's middle-class virtues). His resolution is dialectical: complex and conventional elements operate as simultaneous poles in synthesis, so mind and body, thought and groove, are united rather than opposed, a point he presses against the racialized mind-body binary in writing about rhythm.

Reuland uses YouTube drum covers of 'The Body Electric', 'Subdivisions', and 'YYZ' to analyze Rush's 'aesthetic of replicability': songs built as artifacts meant to be reproduced note-for-note, signaled by literal codes like the Morse-code intro to 'YYZ' and the binary '1001001' the android of 'The Body Electric' must crack to become human. He explains why critics deride this anti-expressive virtuosity by way of Amiri Baraka's racial coding of technique, Pierre Bourdieu's account of how 'natural' taste is legitimated while studied learning bears class stigma, and Mary Bucholtz's picture of nerds as hyper-white; the fans' literal meritocracy parodies the information economy's promise that skill converts directly into success. Finally he reads 'Limelight' as Rush's skepticism toward performance as a 'gilded cage' of inauthenticity, so that play-along videos recode performance as self-improvement that cannot be faked.

Cole pits Plato against Walter Benjamin to vindicate the imitation of Rush: Plato's cave makes art a shadow twice removed from the Forms, and on that view a perfect copy is impossible and every cover degraded, while Peart's 'Limelight' calls the stage a 'gilded cage' that is 'just a prettified cave' yet, with 'we are merely players' (via Shakespeare), makes performing the way out rather than deeper in. Benjamin's translator essay, with its 'language forest' echo and 'pure language', shows how Rush's cover of 'Summertime Blues' on Feedback layers Blue Cheer and the Who into one perception, and how live variations of 'Witch Hunt' and the premature chord of 'Turn the Page' let error overtake and become the new original. The chapter exceeds Aristotle's principle of non-contradiction in 'pure language', where original, copy, and fan covers (Rock Band failures, the South Park 'Lil' Rush' flub, Rick Mercer's drum lesson) are fragments of one greater vessel, so errors are portals of discovery.

book: 058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter
essays: The Only Truly Decent Man Left on the Planet
The Good Life and The Dexter-like Life
You Can’t Help What Happened to You. But You Can Make the Best of It
A Story in Search of a Narrator
You Control Your Urges—They Do Not Control You
The Final Thrust to the Abdomen
A Second Look at Dexter’s Motives
samples: George Reisch's introduction frames the volume with Martha Stout's claim that one in twenty-five people is a conscience-free sociopath who hides in plain sight, arguing that we viewers do the hiding work for them just as Deb, LaGuerta and Batista's assumptions shield Dexter. It presents Dexter's incessant inner questioning as the show's philosophical hook and previews the book's competing verdicts on Harry's Code: monster, Kantian-style model actor, utilitarian good, aesthete, or superhero. It ends by inverting Socrates: normally we point 'know thyself' inward, but the real epistemic danger is the sociopath next door, so our skepticism should aim at the guy in forensics - unless we are ourselves among the one-in-twenty-five, in which case Socrates' injunction to self-examination was spot on.

John Kenneth Muir argues Dexter is best read not as heir to Hannibal Lecter or Patrick Bateman but as a full-blown superhero: his 'impeccable instincts' are a crime-detecting power like Spider-Man's spider-sense or the Shadow's, his gloves, apron and glass visor are a costume, and his 'invisible mask of sympathy' inverts the superhero mask since the Dark Passenger is the true identity. Dexter's orphan origin - Harry lifting the boy from the blood-soaked container - replays the Superman/Batman/Parker template, with the Ice Truck Killer as an amalgam of Riddler and Mr. Freeze who embodies the superhero's shadow potential, and the chapter reads Harry's Code as the American-monomyth vigilante premise that the law can be upheld only by one stepping outside it. The 'killing joke' is that the emotionless sociopath is the only impartial, decent agent of justice in a Miami Metro consumed by passion, and the extra-legal violence question the chapter raises is whether such vigilante force, with its disregard for civil rights, is what justice requires.

Abrol Fairweather uses Dexter as a controlled case study in the philosophy of emotion via Nozick's 'Spock Problem': like Spock, Dexter has beliefs, values and flawless practical reasoning but no emotional feelings, so Mill's Method of Difference lets us isolate what exactly emotions add. Distinguishing 'mere feelings' (beer on the boat, lust for Lila) from emotional feelings that run through our beliefs and values, he adopts Nozick's answer that emotions are value-perceptions - Dexter intellectually recognizes the value of Rita, Deb and his kids but cannot feel it, and that felt value is what his life lacks. Yet Dexter strikes back: he kills because he is too rational rather than too passionate, so whether the Dexter-like life beats the good life depends on whether emotions would help or hinder whatever matters most to us, a question the chapter briefly weighs in Millian terms of the balance of pleasure over pain his meta-killing produces.

Daniel Haas asks whether we can blame Dexter at all if his Dark Passenger is a compulsion formed by the shipping-container trauma he did not choose, and whether consistency then forces us to excuse the Trinity Killer and Ice Truck Killer too. Distinguishing attributive responsibility from accountability, he argues psychopaths cannot be motivated by moral reasons because they lack the moral emotions, and that it was sheer luck whether a traumatized boy landed in Harry's loving home and Code (Dexter) or a mental institution (Brian). Yet Dexter's critical reflection on and revision of Harry's Code, and his willingness to forgo turning himself in to spare Deb, Rita and the kids, paradoxically make him more accountable than ordinary psychopaths and even praiseworthy for his quest to become 'a little wooden boy' who is more human, even if he still deserves to be locked up.

Nicolas Michaud deploys Harry Frankfurt's attack on the principle that blame requires alternative possibilities: through a 'Dex kills Deb' case with a counterfactual intervener and a locked-steering-wheel driver, he shows one can be blameworthy despite having no choice, provided one acts because one wants to. Applied to Dexter, the question is which level of compulsion he has - and since he never truly restrains himself, never turns himself in, and his Season 2 relapse reads as empowerment rather than addiction, he seems to want to want to kill, so Frankfurt's verdict is guilt despite inevitability. The chapter closes with a fictional Princeton encounter where Dexter faces a dilemma - either his victims are blameless compulsives, making him a killer of innocents who violates Harry's Code, or wanting to kill makes them and him blameworthy - and Dexter's choice to kill Frankfurt himself proves he acts freely and is guilty.

Rachel Robison-Greene asks whether Dexter's rule to 'be sure' actually gives him knowledge of his victims' guilt. Distinguishing Cartesian certainty - skeptical hypotheses about deceiving senses, dreams and evil demons, echoing The Matrix - from mere felt certainty, she tests the belief-truth-justification analysis of knowledge traced to Plato against the show: LaGuerta's witness theory fails on belief, Deb's conviction that Neil Perry is the Ice Truck Killer fails on truth, and Astor's accusation of Dexter fails on justification. Neither strong internalism (Dexter straps down Jamie Jaworski without knowing how the murder was done), weak internalism, coherence theory (his false but coherent case against Jonathan Farrow), nor reliabilism (his spidey-sense is explicitly not sufficient by his own admission) captures his practice, so his 'certainty' is just a feeling - and the people on his table may include ones he does not know to be guilty.

essays: Uncertainty, the Dark Side of Learning
Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame
Would Cortana Pass the Turing Test
samples: Fred Van Lente's introduction argues that Master Chief is deliberately an empty shell—faceless, ageless, mostly silent—so the player's identity grafted onto him brings both to life at once in Halo: Combat Evolved's opening cryo-wakeup tutorial. He frames the book with Thoreau's Walden claim that philosophy is living simplicity, mapping it onto the Chief's ascetic soldier existence, and on Socrates: a game worth playing is worth examining, since the unexamined game is not worth playing. He closes with Aristotle's potentiality and actuality: the game actualizes the Chief as a kicker of alien ass, and the book actualizes the series' social and philosophical potential.

Luke Cuddy's editorial introduction traces Halo's ring structures to Larry Niven's Ringworld and Iain M. Banks's Culture orbitals, arguing the series is a genuine literature-game synthesis with a complex backstory (Forerunners, the Covenant, Halo fiction) and not just mindless alien shooting. He accuses Roger Ebert of committing a straw man against videogames as art—judging them from online clips without ever playing—and holds that critics owe any phenomenon a full, honest interpretation before condemning it. The chapter closes by laying out the book's guiding questions (camping, music, Plato, AI, war, Buddhism, Foucault) and warns that philosophy often explores rather than settles them.

Joyce Havstad asks which of the millions of player-instantiated Master Chiefs is real, and whether the flash-cloned John left behind on Eridanus II is the same boy. She runs the Ship of Theseus on the MJOLNIR armor—a technician rebuilds a second suit from every replaced piece—contrasting material with historical continuity, and adds Hobbes's reassembled-planks version. Locke's prince-and-cobbler memory criterion is reconstructed across John, John-117, and Master Chief, then broken by Reid's brave-officer objection, leaving psychological continuity as the best but imperfect criterion; the Flood's conversion of a Covenant soldier into a Combat Form shows identity lost once original sentience is gone.

Jeff Sharpless imagines a Spartan mourning Kurt-051 and asking what his abduction, augmentation, and endless war mean, concluding his life is absurd in Camus's sense: bred as an instrument by the very humanity he is celebrated for saving. Camus's Sisyphus supplies one answer—meaning in the defiant moment of turning back down the hill, which recasts Master Chief's 'I need a weapon' as either hollow absurdity or quiet revolt. Epictetus supplies the alternative: distinguish what is up to us from what is not, withhold assent from impressions like 'we are all going to die,' and the Chief's silence becomes Stoic tranquility—though the chapter concedes Stoicism risks minimizing the injustice done to the Spartan children.

Roger Travis argues Plato would welcome Halo as guardian training: mimesis is really 'playing epic pretend,' and Halo, like the Homeric epics that were Athens' textbooks, trains players in a way of life. Plato's Republic Book 10 critique—the painted bed as copy of a copy of the Form of Bed—warns that playing Master Chief could let appetite rule, yet the Laws' admission that the ideal city's politeia is itself a mimesis turns the tables: the Republic is its own training simulation of philosophic pretend. Re-imagining the cave as prisoners tied to couches playing Super Mario Bros, he argues Halo's dutiful NPCs and waking-to-duty player (literal cryo-wakeups in Combat Evolved and Halo 3) make it philosophy in Plato's own sense, with Aristotle's catharsis leavening the verdict.

Monica Evans asks whether Halo is genuine science fiction or only its iconography—spaceships, aliens, a ringworld borrowed from Niven and Banks—and uses Half-Life 2's City 17 as the contrast case of a game that makes players live its questions about humanity. She finds Halo: Combat Evolved full of trappings but thin on philosophy, its two most human characters being the AIs Cortana and 343 Guilty Spark, whose cheerful willingness to wipe out all sentient life while treasuring archived records marks a truly alien intelligence. Halo 2 gains substance by humanizing the Covenant—the Arbiter's fall and crisis of faith, the Prophets' scheming, the Gravemind's politicking—while the sacrifice arcs of Keyes and Johnson and the Chief's Arthurian ending pull the series toward fantasy as much as science fiction.

book: 060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!
essays: Who Teaches Philosophy Under the Sea
Why Is It the Best Day Ever
How Can I Compete with Geniusness
So, You Tried to Kill Me Over a Little New Age Management, Eh
After All, Who’s the Toughest Critter in Bikini Bottom
That Naive Cube! How Long Must I Suffer This
An Island of Milk and Honey or Rock Bottom
Yours Is Superior, therefore I Concede to You
No Matter How You Flip the Patty . .
Do I Even Care if I’m Dreaming
What You Really Wanted Was Inside You All Along
samples: Editor Joseph Foy's introduction recounts SpongeBob's rise from the 1999 Nickelodeon debut to a global staple (seven Emmys, nine million viewers for 'Atlantis SquarePantis', fans from President Obama to a Mexican 'Bob Esponja Presidente' mural), and argues the show's eight-to-eighty appeal comes from philosophical seeds beneath the whimsy: identity and the self, obligations toward others, the individual in community, principles of the marketplace, and environmental ethics. The volume's stated aim is to use the sponge to kindle interest in philosophy's big questions among fans young and old.

Nicole Pramik argues SpongeBob is Aristotle's self-mastered man: his daily cheerfulness is eudaimonia, a happiness earned by practicing virtue as the mean between vices of excess and deficiency. The chapter tests each mean with episodes — courage between cowardly isolation ('I Had an Accident') and recklessness ('A Life in a Day'), honor between Patrick's under-the-rock humility and Squidward's Easter-Island vanity, honesty in 'Hooky' and 'Wet Painters', and good temper mended with Patrick in 'New Student Starfish' and 'The Fry Cook Games'. His moderation in pleasure and wealth, contrasted with Mr. Krabs's stinginess, and his F.U.N. Song friendship (Aristotle's greatest external good) show the golden mean served up on a sesame seed bun.

Timothy Dunn uses 'Patrick SmartPants', where a brain-coral transplant turns Patrick into a genius who abandons SpongeBob, to ask whether the happy ignoramus or the discontented genius lives better. After sketching a subjectivist defense of Patrick's choice to revert ('knowledge can never replace friendship'), the chapter tests Mill's hedonistic utilitarianism: since competent judges rank higher pleasures qualitatively above lower ones, Mill's dictum that it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied condemns Patrick's destruction of his own higher capacities. Dunn then presses two objections — that people's actual lower-pleasure preferences may be genuine rather than socially produced, and that the capacity for higher pleasure seems worthless without its actual experience — leaving Mill's verdict in tension.

Natasha Liebig reads Squidward as Schopenhauer made flesh: his endless craving for musical fame and revenge on Squilliam exemplifies the blind, irrational will-to-live whose frustration just is suffering, so even success could never satisfy him and others' joys (SpongeBob and Patrick playing) become his bellum omnium. Yet Squidward's clarinet, self-portraits and dance are Schopenhauer's aesthetic escape — will-less contemplation of universal Ideas, with music the most metaphysical art — granting fleeting moments of peace until his neighbors interrupt. The chapter closes on the irony that Schopenhauer's genius is childlike, so SpongeBob and Patrick's effortless wonder may make them the truer artists.

Joseph Foy weighs Mr. Krabs against Ayn Rand's celebration of money-making, Marx's charge that Krabs commodifies his employees — wagering SpongeBob to Plankton in 'Welcome to the Chum Bucket' and working him 43 days without a break in 'Fear of a Krabby Patty' — and Aristotle's and Adam Smith's insistence that wealth is merely instrumental to flourishing. The verdict: Krabs inverts means and ends, fetishizing money until he sells SpongeBob's soul for 62 cents ('Born Again Krabs') and trades his own body for his millionth dollar ('Clams'). His real failing is the unexamined life — he never asks what would actually make him happy — which makes him tragically human rather than simply villainous.

Denise Du Vernay argues Sandy Cheeks is the show's one proof of feminist messaging: a liberal feminist who attains equality within the status quo as scientist, bodybuilder and 'smartest one in Bikini Bottom', while a materialist feminist reading would worry most about SpongeBob's exploitation as Mr. Krabs's worker and property ('Welcome to the Chum Bucket'). She reads 'Squirrel Jokes' as a lesson in how stereotypes spread ('stupidity isn't a virus, but it sure is spreading like one'), catalogs the show's tired female stereotypes (nagging Karen, bratty Pearl), and defends SpongeBob and Sandy against Focus on the Family's 2005 gay-panic attacks as the sexualizing of asexual children's characters.

book: 061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind
essays: His Work Is Its Own Reward
Education never ends Watson. It is a series of lessons with the greatest for
Chapter 8 - The Case of the Dangerous Detective
But the Contradictions! What about the Contradictions
The New Man or the Old
samples: Kate Rufa reads Holmes as Spinoza's 'just man': Watson's 'calculating machine' verdict in The Sign of the Four, his unshaken calm while baiting Moriarty before the Reichenbach leap in 'The Final Problem', and the geometric 'Book of Life' of A Study in Scarlet all show passion mastered by reason into adequate ideas and true freedom. The twist is the cocaine: shooting up between cases means Holmes sacrifices his conatus (the striving to persist in being) to keep his mind at a godlike pitch of activity, a God-complex no finite mode can sustain. Moriarty, equally rational but ruled by passive affects, is the shadow of this ideal, echoing Socrates' Apology point that harming others inevitably harms oneself.

Timothy Sexton argues the real Overman is not Doyle's flat 'calculating machine' but Jeremy Brett's Granada Holmes: the sneer with which he frees the Blue Carbuncle thief and the 'I am not retained by the police' outburst show him stepping beyond the herd's good-and-evil after the death of God. Brett's theatrical style, from the pivot before Lady Brackenstall in 'The Abbey Grange' to 'Gentlemen, we can do better than that' in 'The Norwood Builder', enacts Nietzsche's grand art of giving style to one's character, sublimating nihilistic dread into the pleasure of proving superiority. Where Rathbone-era Sherlocks solve crimes for truth, justice and the Victorian Way, Brett's Holmes makes the work its own reward, satisfying Nietzsche's demand that the Overman 'attain satisfaction with himself'.

J. Solomon Johnson asks whether Holmes's conclusions are knowledge or luck, walking through justified true belief with a Holmesian Gettier case (Watson rightly believing the killer was a former ship hand for the wrong reason), Moore's proof that knowledge entails belief, and Russell's stopped clock as an unsafe belief. BBC Sherlock's fake Vermeer and the 2009 film's 'resurrected' Lord Blackwood illustrate beliefs that fail safety or sensitivity across nearby possible worlds, while 'The Stock-Broker's Clerk' shows Holmes's observation of the scorched slippers making his belief sensitive. The verdict: Holmes is justified by the track record of his own expert methods, a professional billiards player rather than a beginner's-luck fluke, though real-world imitators could never rule out enough alternatives to match him.

Fiona Tomkinson stages a Watson-Holmes dialogue in which Holmes, reworking The Valley of Fear's Birlstone Manor investigation, defines a thing as a thing of no consequence and an object as a thing transformed into a clue: the half-burned candle proving the witnesses lied, the single dumbbell used to sink Baldwin's clothes in the moat, the wedding ring and the hammer, each read through the human fear and care that moved them. A postscript has an aged Watson in 1926 discover Heidegger's newly published Being and Time and recognize his own friend's method in it: Dasein's care and being-toward-death, the directionality of equipment, and the ready-to-hand versus present-at-hand distinction, joking that Holmes might have sued Heidegger for theft of intellectual property.

Sami Paavola and Lauri Jaervilehto reconstruct the textbook on detection Holmes never wrote: following Jaakko Hintikka's interrogative (Socratic) model, where the right question cracks the case, as with the dog that did nothing in the night-time in 'Silver Blaze', and Peirce's triad of deduction, induction and abduction, the backward reasoning from effects to causes exemplified by the Watson-just-from-Afghanistan chain in A Study in Scarlet. They add Peirce's categories of Firstness, Secondness and Thirdness to show Holmes succeeds because he fuses imagination and reverie with fieldwork, experiment and exact inference. The chapter closes with a twelve-point practical toolbox distilled from the canon.

Francine Sanders, a former Chicago police-misconduct investigator, rereads the 1939-46 Rathbone films (The Secret Weapon, The Spider Woman, The Woman in Green) against the hard-boiled world of Chandler and Hammett. Holmes's tea-pouring intimacy with Watson, his disguises (book peddler, roughneck sailor, bogus postman after faking his death), his puzzle-obsession rather than femme-fatale obsession with Adrea Spedding, and the closing vigil over a London where 'women can come and go in safety' mark him as the hopeful, partnered opposite of the alienated loner of noir, whose corrupt city always wins.

book: 062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For
essays: Who’s Putting Ideas in Your Head
Legal and Not So Legal Forms of Inception
Does the Top Fall Does It Matter in the End
Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word
An Old Man, Filled with Regret . .
Guilt Can be a Real Bitch
samples: The book's introduction frames Inception around two threats to the self: the old Cartesian doubt that we can never be sure we are not dreaming, and a newer neuroscience-based worry that even our thoughts are not our own because we act on them before we become aware of them. It surveys the volume's guiding questions - whether inception, unlike the implants of Blade Runner and Dark City, is a wrong akin to propaganda, advertising or brainwashing; whether Second Life-style virtual worlds mean walking away from reality; and whether even 'true inspiration' can be faked. It also previews the book's boldest readings, such as the theory that the whole film is Cobb's single dream on the flight and the claim that the dreams run on a server, making Mal into 'Mal-ware'.

Wenmackers uses Inception's dream levels and its ambiguous spinning-top ending as a guided tour of skeptical philosophy, diagramming how dreams-within-dreams, kicks, Limbo and exponentially dilated dream time work. She tests the totem against Zhuangzi's butterfly and lucid-dreaming reality checks, then runs Plato's Cave and the eternal Forms, Descartes's cogito and evil demon, Putnam's brain-in-a-vat, and Nozick's experience machine to ask whether Cobb's world - or ours - is real. Her conclusion is Socratic ('know that you know nothing'): subjective reality feels equally real on every level and the top level can never be known. She even argues that dream-time dilation means Cobb should not kill himself while in doubt, since real time barely passes, so a little philosophy rescues the happy ending.

Brogaard argues Inception's dream technology is closer to real neuroscience than it looks: against Hobson's activation-synthesis model (with Dennett's picture of dreams as narratives concocted on waking) she cites Foulkes, Antrobus and Solms to locate dreaming in dopamine-driven frontal motivation areas, so the film's streamlined plot-driven shared dreams cannot be ruled out. LaBerge's lucid-dream mask shows dream content can be manipulated, split-brain research plus transcranial magnetic stimulation suggests how one mind could tap another's right hemisphere, and the 'embedded dreams' are best read as a single dream whose deeper layers surface as the subject's own beliefs let his guard down. She closes with the legal and illegal inception we already practice: salesmen's mind games and fear conditioning via a temporarily deactivated hippocampus.

Andersen contends Inception goes one deeper than Descartes: where the dream argument threatened only the external world, inception threatens the autonomy of thought itself, since the 'core conception' that defines identity - Fischer's reading of his father's dying word 'disappointed' - can be implanted. Tracing Nolan's obsession with thought-manipulation through his earlier films (the manipulator Cobb of Following, Leonard's self-deception in Memento, the Joker's schemes), he shows inception as co-opting subjectivity. Against the Cartesian answer of doubting everything, the fates of Mal and Cobb in Limbo - where doubt, once planted, grows devastatingly, and where a totem cannot guard against self-deception - teach that the way back to reality is the leap of trust in others: only by opening himself to Ariadne, Miles and his children can Cobb turn away from the top and go home.

Rennett tests Cobb's choice to leave Limbo against Nozick's three reasons for refusing the experience machine: we want to actually do things (raise his real children, not loving projections), to be a certain kind of person (Yusuf's dream-den addicts are 'indeterminate blobs'), and to touch something deeper than a man-made world. He then recruits Berkeley's esse est percipi to explain Mal's sincerity - she perceives Limbo and remembers it, so for her it is real - and argues that shared dreams differ from private dreams and the experience machine because they leave waking traces, like Mal's bullet in Arthur's leg. The chapter ends by making reality a matter of choice: like the cave prisoners of Plato's allegory, each character believes a world, and Cobb's ignoring of the top is his choice to live in the world with his children.

Testerman turns inception against itself: Cobb and Saito believe they freely plan the Fischer job, but conscious will is a feeling, not a cause. From William James's effortful attention and Dewey's willpower she moves to Penfield's stimulated patients and Libet's readiness-potential experiments showing the brain prepares action before we feel we will it, so Fischer, Cobb and Saito are all equally 'incepted' by subconscious forces - 'freedom is ignorance of the causes of actions', as she glosses Spinoza, with Hume's point that causality is only inferred. Advertising, the foot-in-the-door effect and subliminal primes already do inception's work more cheaply, and the team's 'group will' flows from Saito's own unexamined drive for power, so against Socrates she concludes the unexamined life is perfectly suitable for living.

book: 063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits
essays: We Can Conceive It for Ourselves Wholesale
Free Will at the Box Office
Show Me What You’re Made Of
Have You Ever Retired a Human by Mistake
Do You Think Androids Have Souls
We Can Endorse That for You Wholesale
From Hover Cars to Substance D
samples: Ethan Mills opens his 'investigation' of Hollywood's Dick adaptations (Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, The Adjustment Bureau) by insisting that fan complaints signal something essential lost in translation from print to film, not mere infidelity. He frames the issue as a clash between two philosophical worldviews about free will and knowledge, adopting a bounty-hunter persona to hunt down what Hollywood changed.

Mills defines the 'Holly-worldview' (good defeats evil, free will secures the triumph of the human spirit, heroes discover truth before the credits roll) and opposes it to the Dickian worldview of paranoia, ignorance and accepted unfreedom, where a 'happy ending' means accepting some inevitable, possibly depressing fact about our place in the universe. He announces the chapter's plan: to test whether the Holly-worldview survives Dick's challenges to its two tenets, free will and knowledge.

Mills contrasts Dick's 'The Minority Report', where Anderton knowingly kills Kaplan exactly as the final Precog prediction foretold and accepts exile contentedly, with Spielberg's film in which Agatha insists 'You still have a choice' and Crow is spared. He pairs 'Adjustment Team', where Ed Fletcher grovels and accepts the adjustments as for the greater good, with The Adjustment Bureau, where Damon's love teaches the Chairman a lesson and wins the couple their freedom. In both cases the story doubts free will while the movie insists the hero's choice secures human dignity, which Mills attributes to the Dickian worldview being box-office poison rather than to mere economics.

Mills separates determinism from fate: the film's Chairman and his angels override a free humanity, while 'Adjustment Team' depicts an if-then causal order with nothing supernatural being circumvented. He lays out hard determinism (choices caused by brain states and bad noodles leave you 'no better off than an android with false memories') against soft determinism, enlisting Hume's point that without predictable behavior laws like stop signs would be ridiculous. A free action, he argues, needs no uncaused cause: it is unconstrained and flows from your character, as with Anderton's choice to run.

Mills uses the Blade Runner cuts to stage skepticism: the theatrical happy ending hides the question, the Director's Cut unicorn hints Scott wants Deckard to be a replicant, but Dick's novel has Luba Luft tell Deckard 'You must be an android' and presses him on whether his Voigt-Kampff memories are false, leaving the question unresolved for the reader and for Deckard himself. Since any evidence (empathy, the test's own accuracy) can itself be doubted, the novel is more radically skeptical than the films, because it makes both hypotheses compatible with all the evidence. He then shows Ubik pushing this to the limit, where characters cannot tell what year it is, whether their money is real, or even whether they are alive or dead.

Mills argues that for the ancient skeptics skepticism was the cure, not the disease: Sextus Empiricus prescribes setting equally strong arguments against each other until judgment is suspended and tranquility follows. He reads Nagarjuna and Jayarashi as more radical, using contradictions to uproot the very impulse to hold philosophical views at all, weaning themselves from attachment even to Buddhist views. Applied to Dick, both approaches would have us stop agonizing over whether Deckard is an android or the Ubik characters are dead: the best way to stop worrying is to stop wanting the answers.
